messages.author: 97d82fedb7016adb
messages.subject: warmup for the lazy
parts:
Hi!

I was just wondering under what conditions I can go with a diagonal (unit) mass matrix: To my understanding, the diagonal of the mass matrix should be the variances of my parameters in the posterior. So if I have good reasons to assume that I know beforehand the variances of my parameters in my posterior, then I could scale my variables and skip a lot of effort during warmup right?

What would left to be done during warmup? I.e. assuming the above works, what is the least number of steps during warmup to get likely good sampling parameters?

Thanks!

Best,
Sebastian

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] warmup for the lazy
parts:
We've rarely seen any performance gain with a dense
mass matrix.

When we estimate the mass matrix, we use the inverse of
a regularized sample covariance from the last half of the
draws from warmup in exponentially increasing block sizes.
There's a description in the part of the manual about algorithms.

The other piece of warmup is step size tuning for the target
acceptance rate. That's it --- once you have those, there's
nothing else. So yes, that could conceivably save all of your warmup.
Or you could give it a good starting point and let it work from there.
But that might not work as set up because we have to go from wherever
the initialization is at to the typical set (high mass volume of the
posterior), and the curvature may vary.

We're going to let users specify mass matrix plus step size, either fixed
or as initializations, but right now, there's no way to input them in any
of our interfaces.

Scaling variables so they're all unit scale in the posterior would
eliminate the need to estimate a mass matrix --- you could use the unit mass
matrix.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] warmup for the lazy
parts:
I’m skeptical of that strategy.  I’m guessing that ADVI will be better as a straight approximation, than as a shrotcut to warmup.

I wouldn’t be surprised if the warmup process can be improved, I’m just guessing that the improving-the-warmup process will require more direct grappling with HMC, also I remain optimistic about approaches in which we use multiple chains to develop multiple mass matrices and then Stan can cycle between them to avoid the worst-case behavior that is sometimes killing us.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] warmup for the lazy
parts:
If warmup could be improved - that would be great!

One advantage of somehow figuring out the scale and then re-scaling variables would be that this information can be saved across many runs. Redoing the warmup over and over again is very wasteful. I know, that this also requires sensible inits as other wise things go wrong which makes it a chicken - egg problem.

Does the performance of Stan degrade substantially if I scale with a somewhat "too large" scale than what would be optimal? If so, then one could scale to this and somewhat relax the requirements on initialization.

Yet another approach would be to use an approximate scheme first, define with this a proposal density, then do full Bayes and finally re-sample using IS.

Sebastian

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] warmup for the lazy
parts:
> On Oct 7, 2015, at 3:45 AM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> If warmup could be improved - that would be great!
>
> One advantage of somehow figuring out the scale and then re-scaling variables would be that this information can be saved across many runs. Redoing the warmup over and over again is very wasteful.

The motivation for multiple runs is to make sure we
converge from diffuse starting points. That means redoing
warmup.
> I know, that this also requires sensible inits as other wise things go wrong which makes it a chicken - egg problem.

The chicken and egg problem is that adaptation is often
required to find the typical set, but you want to adapt
only to the typical set after you find it. That's why we
only use the second half of warmup iterations to train the
mass matrix (reduces to variable scaling with the default
diagonal mass matrices).
> Does the performance of Stan degrade substantially if I scale with a somewhat "too large" scale than what would be optimal?

Yes. It can cause the integrator to be so bad that
Stan devolves to random-walk Metropolis. Erring on the
too-small side is much safer in that it's less likely
to kill the flow that makes HMC so efficient.

> If so, then one could scale to this and somewhat relax the requirements on initialization.
>
> Yet another approach would be to use an approximate scheme first, define with this a proposal density, then do full Bayes and finally re-sample using IS.

There's lots of open research to do out there. And
we have a nice way to evaluate it with our modeling
language in case anyone wants to do it.

- Bob

messages.author: 97d82fedb7016adb
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] warmup for the lazy
parts:
Hi!

Currently, Stan always starts from scratch which is a safe choice, but waste the information we already have. Modeling proceeds by altering the model (most of the time in small steps) and by altering between smaller and larger data sets (to do fast model build-up and then have once in a while a "full" but slow run).

Hence, both processes (model build-up) and data alteration can be viewed as a perturbation to what one has. As a consequence, the perturbed system by which I refer to parameters and tuning parameters will be within the vicinity of where we already are. Therefore, there is no need to start from scratch again - which saves a lot of time. Of course, one needs to be aware of the dangers such an approach entails, i.e. starting from scratch once in a while is an important consistency/stability check of the model.

To some degree I can take advantage of the above thought be being "informative" with the initials, doing so with the tuning parameters is the logic next step and it is great to hear that this is on its way.

But, I see, I am jumping ahead of what is in the works.

Sebastian

If you were only perturbing the system then the data would only be changing
incrementally from run to run.  But it’s not — you’re going from small data to
large data, a huge change that can cause non-perturbative changes to the
posterior and hence the adaptation tuning.

messages.author: 97d82fedb7016adb
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] warmup for the lazy
parts:
Yup, scale is nasty to handle. From my own experience in a totally different settings, it was important to make sure that scale does not get too small too quickly.

Anyway, if you have a regularized point estimate, then giving (advanced) users control over the regularization would be great I think. This should then come very close to what I would like to do. I know, I jump ahead here, but if this is possible to include into future designs, that would be very useful I think.

Sebastian

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] warmup for the lazy
parts:
Absolutely. User control of regularization is on the
to-do list. It should show up for Stan 3. We're (mostly
Daniel and Michael) refactoring the Stan/interface API.
That should make this all easier to do in a way that's
consistent across interfaces. What's holding us back now is
that all of this needs to be implemented five or
six times --- once for each interface.

- Bob

messages.author: 37f85c6188fe5eeb
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] warmup for the lazy
parts:
On Thursday, October 8, 2015 at 12:56:25 AM UTC-7, Sebastian Weber wrote:
Hi!

Currently, Stan always starts from scratch which is a safe choice, but waste the information we already have. Modeling proceeds by altering the model (most of the time in small steps) and by altering between smaller and larger data sets (to do fast model build-up and then have once in a while a "full" but slow run).

Hence, both processes (model build-up) and data alteration can be viewed as a perturbation to what one has. As a consequence, the perturbed system by which I refer to parameters and tuning parameters will be within the vicinity of where we already are. Therefore, there is no need to start from scratch again - which saves a lot of time. Of course, one needs to be aware of the dangers such an approach entails, i.e. starting from scratch once in a while is an important consistency/stability check of the model.

To some degree I can take advantage of the above thought be being "informative" with the initials, doing so with the tuning parameters is the logic next step and it is great to hear that this is on its way.

One possibility is to do your run with normal warmup, get your posterior values, and then rescale your model, and provide the rescaled posterior mean values as the initial positions for doing further runs with your extra data or perturbed model. The goal would be at least to reduce the number of warmup samples since you'd probably be starting in the typical set, and you'd have a mass matrix that's closer to a unit diagonal.

This is more or less just an efficiency hack, but it could be a big one. One thing I've definitely found is that when I build my models in dimensionless form to begin with and use my knowledge to rescale the variables so that they are all O(1) my Stan models run without many hitches. If you don't have info about your variable's scales, a single initial run of Stan could get you the info you need to rescale your model.

This is kind of the dual process to inputting an initial mass matrix, alter the model via pure rescaling so an initial unit diagonal mass matrix is already a good starting point.
